redaction.purpose.body:
After a target's content has been erased, an operator can remove that content from the ledger's history. The history keeps its shape: every revision and every record position stays, and only the target's content goes. Afterwards, no record, revision field or ledger index reachable through IVG holds the target's IDs, values or messages.

- Known exceptions: records the run cannot attribute to the target ([unattributed](#redaction.unattributed)), reifier delete records reached by neither target ([target nodes](#redaction.target.nodes)), actor fields, which are [kept by design](#redaction.metadata.actor), and IVG's own snapshot archives and pre-upgrade ledger rows ([other copies](#redaction.out-of-reach.other-copies)).
- Live stores outside the ledger are erasure's job; today search indexes can still answer with erased text ([erasure](erasure.g5.md#erasure.scope)).

redaction.target.body:
A target is a graph, optionally narrowed to the entity IDs that begin with a prefix and its separator.

- The separator is part of the match, so the prefix `acme` never matches `acme-health|…`.
- A prefix that already ends with the separator is used as given.
- An empty separator is refused.

redaction.target.nodes.body:
The ledger records every node in the default graph ([node scope](ledger.g5.md#ledger.node-scope)). So a tenant's node records can be reached only through an ID prefix with the default graph as the target. A named-graph target reaches relationship, qualifier and temporal-edge records, but never node records.

- A relationship delete, or a detach delete of a node, also deletes the relationship's reifier nodes. Inside the tenant's own revision, their delete records carry each reifier's own ID, the default graph and a snapshot of its labels and properties. Unless a reifier ID begins with the tenant's prefix, neither of the tenant's two targets reaches these records.

redaction.target.relationships.body: With a prefix, a relationship record belongs to the target when the relationship's source or target ID begins with the match. A qualifier change belongs to the target when its relationship does.

redaction.tenant.body:
Fully redacting a tenant whose relationships live in its own graph takes two targets: the tenant's graph, and the tenant's prefix in the default graph.

- Erase the tenant's nodes first with the prefix and its separator, such as `tenant|`. Erasing by prefix has no separator rule, so `tenant` alone would also erase other tenants' nodes ([prefix match](erasure.g5.md#erasure.prefix-match)).
- Keep each tenant's temporal edges in its own graph. Spec 256 put off erasing one tenant's temporal data inside a shared graph, and a prefix erase misses its temporal-only events ([open question](#redaction.after-erasure.temporal)).

redaction.call.body:
A redaction call names the graph (none means the default graph), an optional prefix, the separator, an actor and a batch size, and may cap the number of batches. The defaults are separator `|`, actor `system:ledger-redact` and 2,000 tombstones per batch. Two calls are the same redaction when they name the same graph and the same match string, the prefix with its separator, so `acme` and `acme|` name one target.

- A refusal raises a typed error: `RedactionTargetLiveError`, `RedactionInProgressError`, `InvalidRedactionTargetError`, `LedgerNotEnabledError`, `LedgerDisabledError`, `LedgerTransactionOpenError` or `LedgerLockTimeoutError`.
- An unexpected failure inside a batch raises `LedgerInconsistencyError`, and that batch is rolled back.
- A refusal before the first batch changes nothing. A refusal between batches, such as `LedgerDisabledError` or `LedgerLockTimeoutError`, keeps the earlier batches and the marker; running the same call again finishes the run.

redaction.after-erasure.body:
Redaction only follows erasure. It is refused while any row of the target is live, because replaying the history without the target's records would no longer match the store.

- The refusal names the live target and changes nothing.
- Liveness is checked again, under the ledger lock, just before the run finishes.

redaction.after-erasure.default-graph.body:
For a default-graph target, live node, label and property rows count in every graph, because the ledger's node records and verify both ignore graphs. Relationship rows count only in the target graph.

- So the whole default graph, with no prefix, cannot be redacted while any graph holds a node.

redaction.after-erasure.temporal.body:
Should the target's temporal-index entries count as live? There is no provisional answer.

- Today only table rows count, so a target whose temporal edges have no plain relationship row (temporal-only predicates) can be redacted while those edges remain.
- Possible answers: count temporal entries as live; or rely on erasure, which removes them only when the tenant has its own graph or the events are erased by ID. A prefix erase leaves temporal-only events whose endpoints have no node row.
- Spec 256 put off erasing one tenant's temporal data inside a shared graph, because with one graph per tenant a graph erase covers it.

redaction.strict-mode.body:
How should an operator erase and redact a tenant while strict mode is on? There is no provisional answer.

- Strict mode refuses the engine's erase methods, so the erase-first rule cannot be met without turning strict mode off.
- Possible answers: let erasure run under strict mode; record an erase as a ledger operation; or document turning strict mode off for the erase.

redaction.tombstone.body: Each of the target's records becomes a tombstone at its own position. The tombstone keeps the kind of change, the entity kind and the record's flags, and holds the SHA-256 of the original canonical record. It holds no entity ID, attribute, value or graph.

redaction.tombstone.digest.body: For now the digest is unsalted, so an auditor who holds the original canonical record can prove it was the one redacted. A guessable record, such as a short ID with a known shape, can be confirmed by guessing; the digest does not hide it.

redaction.tombstone.digest-source.body:
Which copy of a record must an auditor keep to recompute its digest? Provisional answer: the server's canonical record, captured before the redaction.

- Only the server's canonical form is known to reproduce the digest.
- The Python reader spells a genesis default-graph relationship's graph differently, and exports carry no records.

redaction.tombstone.canonical-form.body: The canonical record is a JSON object with the record's fields in alphabetical order: attribute, entity ID, entity kind, flags (a list), graph, new value, change kind, ordinal, prior value and seq. An absent value and an empty graph are written as null, and seq and ordinal are numbers. The digest is the SHA-256 of that text in UTF-8, written as lowercase hex.

redaction.readers.body: Replay, diff and reconstruction treat a tombstone as contributing nothing. Record readers show a tombstone as a redacted change at its position instead of hiding the position. A diff lists the positions of the tombstones in its range.

redaction.unattributed.body:
What should happen to a record in the target graph when it cannot be determined whether the record belongs to a prefix target? There is no provisional answer.

- Today it is left in place and counted in the receipt, and the run still reports complete.
- Possible answers: block completion until it is resolved; tombstone it; or keep today's behavior and document it.

redaction.metadata.body: A revision with any redacted record loses its message, source, correlation ID and idempotency key, even when its other records belong to another tenant. Its seq, revision ID, parent, kind and commit time stay, and so do the other graphs' records.

redaction.metadata.exception.body: Clearing those four fields is the only change ever allowed to a revision row. It is allowed only to the redaction itself, for a revision that already has a tombstone, and only to empty those fields. Every other update and every delete is still refused.

redaction.metadata.actor.body: A revision's actor, actor type and connection user are kept, because they identify the writer, not the tenant. A deployment that puts tenant names in the actor must choose another actor.

redaction.idempotency.body: The idempotency key of each revision that gets a tombstone is unbound and kept only as a digest. A later commit with that key is refused, so a retry can neither replay the redacted revision nor re-create the erased content.

redaction.idempotency.other-tenant.body: When a revision spans tenants, should the other tenant also lose its retry protection and its correlation-ID lookup for that revision? Today it does, as a side effect of clearing the shared revision's fields. Provisional answer: yes, as part of the accepted cost of clearing on any redacted record, although only the lost message was weighed.

redaction.audit.body: A finished redaction adds one revision of kind `redaction` to the ledger. It names each redacted revision by seq with its number of tombstones, and holds counts and a digest of the target instead of the target's name. Nothing in it comes from the target.

redaction.out-of-reach.body: Copies outside the ledger keep the content: exports written before the redaction, IRIS journals and backups. Every receipt says so.

redaction.out-of-reach.other-copies.body: Should the receipt also name IVG's own snapshot archives and the older ledger rows that an upgrade to a new schema leaves behind? Both can hold ledger content that a redaction does not reach. Provisional answer: name them in the receipt and the documentation.

redaction.batches.body:
A redaction runs in bounded batches, and an in-progress marker records it while it is unfinished. Each batch is one transaction under the ledger's head lock.

- The final step, in its own transaction, re-checks liveness, removes the target's statement entries, writes the redaction revision and removes the marker.
- Each batch holds the lock briefly; the performance target is a [child](#redaction.batches.speed).

redaction.batches.readers.body:
While the marker exists, record readers, diffs, reconstructions and exports refuse with `RedactionInProgressError`, and verify reports `redaction_in_progress` and adopts nothing.

- History, statistics and the SQL `ledger_records` procedure still answer and can show a half-redacted ledger. Whether they must also refuse is open.

redaction.batches.commits.body: While the marker exists, a commit with any record in the target is refused, and other commits proceed. Today a record whose attribution to the target is unknown, such as a qualifier whose statement endpoints are not known, is let through.

redaction.batches.competing.body: A redaction of a different target is refused, with nothing changed, until the unfinished one completes.

redaction.batches.resume.body:
Running the same redaction again resumes an unfinished run. Running a finished redaction again changes nothing and reports zero. A caller may stop a run after a set number of batches and resume it later.

- If the ledger is disabled between batches, the run stops, keeps its marker and resumes after the ledger is enabled again.

redaction.batches.abort.body: Can an unfinished redaction be abandoned? Today a run whose target became live again can finish only after the target is erased again, and until then the marker blocks readers, verify and other targets. Provisional answer: no abort; erase again and resume.

redaction.batches.marker-text.body: While a run is unfinished, the marker holds the target in plain text so that commits can be checked against it. The marker is removed when the run finishes, but IRIS journals keep it.

redaction.batches.speed.body: On the laptop's enterprise container, redacting a tenant with 100,000 records should take under a minute and block commits for under one second at a time.

redaction.verify.body: After a target is erased and redacted, verify reports equal again; after the erase alone it reports a divergence. This holds when the ledger matched the store before the erase, nothing was written outside the ledger after it, and the redacted targets cover everything that was erased.

structure.write.body:
Each engine write is its own transaction when the caller has none, and a nested part of the caller's open transaction otherwise. If the write fails, only its own part is taken back; the caller's commit or rollback decides the rest. These kinds of call are the exceptions:

- Calls that cannot be part of one transaction refuse a caller's open transaction and commit in steps: snapshot restore and the bulk loader.
- Some calls use the engine's own native connection: erasing a graph or every graph, a rebuild, switching multigraph mode, named search-index writes (BM25 and vector indexes), temporal purges, rebuilds and settings, and FHIR graph calls. They join the caller's transaction only when the engine was made on the caller's own connection; with `from_connect` they commit on their own ([erasure](erasure.g5.md#erasure.atomic)). Whether this should depend on how the engine was opened is [open](#structure.write.engine-connection).
- Deleting nodes removes the reifier nodes of their edges in later transactions.
- Temporal writes follow their own rule ([temporal writes](temporal.g5.md#temporal.write)).

structure.write.engine-connection.body:
Should whether a write joins the caller's transaction depend on how the engine was opened? There is no provisional answer.

- Today the calls that use the engine's own native connection nest in the caller's transaction for an engine made on the caller's connection, and commit on their own for an engine made with `from_connect`.
- Plausible answers: make every such call join the caller's transaction, refuse an open caller transaction, or document the difference per call.

structure.node.body:
`create_node` changes nothing and reports False when the node already exists in its graph. A write that IRIS refuses raises an error and leaves nothing behind.

- When two callers create the same node at once, one creates it and the other reports False.
- A new node gets an `id` property equal to its ID unless the caller gives one. The ledger reserves that property name ([changesets](ledger.g5.md#ledger.changeset)).

structure.node.bulk.body:
`bulk_create_nodes` returns the accepted input IDs in order, including repeats and nodes already present. It skips IDs that Python treats as empty, including 0, False, None and empty text; each node's own graph value wins over the call's graph, and None names the default graph.

- Existing nodes gain labels and property keys they lack and keep the values they already hold. Before adding any node row, the batch removes properties left for its IDs whose node row is missing in that graph; repeated IDs then merge into the first occurrence, and other graphs stay unchanged.
- A None-valued property is omitted. An absent `id` property defaults to the node ID; an explicit None-valued `id` property is omitted too. [Node reads](#structure.node.read) apply the shared type and alias rules.
- A SQL batch that leaves indexes in place checks every expected parent, label and non-null property key before returning. A missing required row or failed write raises and takes back that SQL operation under the database transaction contract; an existing property's different value is a permitted merge.
- The native loader's chunk commits and index drop/rebuild follow the separate [bulk-load boundary](../concepts/install.g5.md#install.bulk_load); the SQL rollback rule does not establish those guarantees.

structure.node.delete.body:
Deleting a node removes, in its graph, its labels, properties, documents, vectors and incident edges, and then the reifier nodes of those edges.

- The node and its own rows go in one transaction.
- Without a named graph, the delete uses the one graph that holds the ID ([graph scope](../concepts/graph-scope.g5.md#graph.default)).

structure.node.delete.bulk.body:
Bulk node deletion drops None and empty IDs, converts the rest to text and removes repeats, then runs batches in each selected graph; a failed batch is logged and later batches still run. Its `DeleteResult` reports `deleted` from calls that returned successfully and `failed` as the number of requested IDs in calls that raised; converting it to an integer or boolean uses only `deleted`.

- A true result can have failures. A false result does not prove that nothing was deleted: a node delete can finish before its later reifier cleanup raises, and the caller counts that whole batch as failed.
- The same risk applies when an underlying store call commits some chunks before a later chunk fails ([erasure atomicity](erasure.g5.md#erasure.atomic)). The batch log's claim that everything rolled back is too strong.
- With an explicit graph only that graph is selected. With graph omitted, an ID held in several graphs is refused before any deletion.

structure.node.update.body:
Writing a node with `store_node` creates its row if it is missing and always reports True.

- Each property it is given replaces that property's value; a None value removes the property, and other properties stay.
- Each label it is given is added; existing labels stay.
- The node gets an `id` property equal to its ID only when it has none yet.
- The row, properties and labels are one transaction, and a duplicate node or label is not an error.

structure.node.read.body:
`get_node` and `get_nodes` read the named graph, or the default graph when none is named, using that graph's labels and typed properties. Batched results follow the requested ID order and preserve repeated IDs; an existing node with no labels or properties is returned, while an absent ID with no child rows is omitted (`get_node` returns None).

- Properties named `id` and `labels` are returned as `p_id` and `p_labels`, keeping the structural ID and label list intact. If the caller also stored `p_id` or `p_labels`, today's flat result loses one value according to property row order; see [the unresolved alias rule](#structure.node.read.aliases).
- A node with child rows is included without a separate node-row check; orphan child rows can therefore appear as a node. Reads fail if a database read fails, rather than returning a fabricated empty node.

structure.node.read.aliases.body: How should the flat node read preserve both `id` and `p_id` properties (and both `labels` and `p_labels`)? Working answer: preserve every stored property in a separate property map; the alternative is a documented reserved alias namespace with validation before writing. Today either colliding property can win, while the structural fields remain intact; the product owner must choose the compatible API change.

structure.edge.body: An edge connects two nodes of the same graph and may carry qualifiers. Creating an edge adds any missing endpoint to that graph in the same transaction, so a failed edge leaves no node behind.

structure.edge.single.body: Outside multigraph mode a graph holds at most one ordinary edge per triple. An ordinary duplicate changes no edge values: `create_edge` reports False, while `store_edge` accepts it and reports True; neither treats it as an error.

structure.edge.weight.body: An edge's weight lives in its qualifiers, so the adjacency index, a rebuild and Cypher's `r.weight` all read the same value. An edge with no weight costs 1.0 in weighted walks.

structure.edge.weight.set.body: `set_edge_weight` changes the weight of an existing edge in the default graph only. It updates every edge of the triple in one transaction, and reports False, writing nothing, when the default graph has no such edge.

structure.edge.delete.body: Deleting an edge removes the triple's edges from one graph, or from every graph when the caller asks for that. It reports success even when nothing matched, and a delete that IRIS refuses raises an error and removes nothing.

structure.edge.delete.reifications.body: Should deleting an edge also remove its reifications and edge embeddings, as deleting a node, deleting a relationship through the ledger, and erasing edges do? No source decides it, and there is no provisional answer.

structure.reification.body:
A reifier node holds properties about one edge row, and each reifier belongs to exactly one edge.

- Reifying an edge creates the reifier node in the default graph, whatever the edge's graph, labels it, links it to the edge and adds each given property the node lacks, all in one transaction.
- Reifying an edge that does not exist writes nothing and returns no reifier.
- Reading an edge's reifications returns each reifier with its properties.
- Deleting a reifier removes its link, properties, labels and node rows in every graph, and leaves the edge in place.

structure.multigraph.body: Multigraph mode is a per-graph setting, off by default and available for the default graph too. In it, two nodes may hold several edges of one type, as openCypher's `CREATE` expects, and each edge keeps its own identity.

structure.multigraph.off.body: With the mode off, a graph behaves exactly as before multigraph mode existed, with the same storage, generated SQL and adjacency layout. Every writer uses edge key 0, so such a graph holds at most one edge row per triple.

structure.multigraph.switch.body: Turning multigraph mode on is always allowed. Turning it off is refused while any triple of the graph holds more than one edge, and erasing a graph clears its mode.

structure.multigraph.layout.body:
A triple with one edge looks the same in the adjacency index in either mode.

- While a triple has two or more edges, each edge also has its own entry, and the triple records how many edges it holds.
- The triple's own entry carries the weight of its edge with the lowest edge key.
- Edge keys are never renumbered, and a live edge's key is never reused.
- A new edge takes one more than the triple's highest live key, or 0 for the first, so the key of a deleted highest edge can return.
- When two writers pick the same new key, the loser retries once with a fresh key and fails loudly after a second clash.
- A rebuild produces the same layout as the writes that led to it.

structure.multigraph.count.body:
Degree counts every edge of a multigraph triple, while the interned snapshot keeps one entry per triple. Edge embeddings stay per triple, so parallel edges share one.
- A one-hop read answers one row per relationship. Two edges of one type between the same two nodes are two rows, and `count()` counts both.
- The one-hop ID shortcut keeps this rule: it repeats a target once for each edge the triple holds.
- Cypher tells relationships apart by edge ID, so two equal parallel edges stay two; asking for distinct answers folds them.

structure.multigraph.create_edge.body: In a multigraph, should `create_edge` always add a new edge, and should a variant return the new edge's ID? The provisional answer, from the multigraph specification, is yes to both.

structure.multigraph.ledger.body: How does the revision ledger name one of several parallel edges? The provisional answer, from the multigraph specification, is that a reference may carry the edge key, and a reference that fits several edges is refused as ambiguous. Today the ledger acts on the first matching row and deletes the surviving edges' adjacency (observed).

structure.multigraph.restore.body: A restore brings back each graph's multigraph mode with its edges, so a restored multigraph keeps its parallel edges, their layout and their counts.

structure.adjacency.body: The adjacency index is derived from the edge and label rows, which stay authoritative. Every entry is keyed by its graph ([graph keys](../concepts/graph-scope.g5.md#graph.key)).

structure.adjacency.declared.body: Where the index is declared, every row insert, update or delete, by any path, changes it in the same transaction. A rollback undoes both, and the index holds no entry without a row behind it.

structure.adjacency.undeclared.body: Where the index is not declared, such as after a setup that did not finish, only the engine's own edge writers and a rebuild keep it current. Cypher writes, `store_edge` and the store's `write_edges` leave it stale until a rebuild.

structure.adjacency.one_writer.body: One module makes every change to the out-edge and in-edge entries, so the rules every such change must follow are written once. A source scan fails on any other writer unless an explicit, justified exception is added.

structure.adjacency.declare.body:
Setup declares the two adjacency indexes only once their prerequisites exist, declares each one once, and leaves an index that is already declared alone.
- Nothing is declared while the callback classes are not compiled, while the schema's own procedure class is not compiled, before the edge table has its edge key column, or before both tables have the graph column. Setup skips with a reason, and a later setup declares them.
- Once every prerequisite exists, both are declared: the edge index first, then the label index.
- An index already declared as the adjacency index is left alone. A plain index with the same name is dropped and replaced.
- Before the edge index is built, every triple that has temporal events but no row gets its marked row. The build then fills the index from every row, which also repairs drift.

structure.degree.body: A node's degree is counted from the adjacency index when asked and is never kept as a stored counter. A stored counter cannot stay exact when transactions roll back, and no reader needs one.

structure.degree.cache.body: A counted degree may be cached and served while the node's generation has not moved since the count. Every change to a node's outgoing adjacency moves its generation, and deleting the cache changes no answer.

structure.degree.cache.uncommitted.body:
A cached degree never includes an edge that was later rolled back.

- Each graph has one writer lock. Writers hold it shared, so writers never wait for each other, and keep it until their transaction ends.
- A reader stores its count only when it could take that lock alone at once, and the node's generation did not move while it counted.
- A writer that cannot get the lock within 5 seconds still writes, and turns degree caching off for its graph until the next rebuild.

structure.degree.cache.erase.body: Erasing a node or a graph clears its generations and cached degrees. No count cached before the erase may be served after it, even when later writes bring the generation back to an earlier value.

structure.degree.cache.warm.body:
A rebuild leaves the degree cache filled, so the first reads after it do not recount.

- Standalone `WarmAll(graph)` also fills graphs that exist only in adjacency globals: it enumerates that graph's outgoing sources directly, without SQL node or edge rows. It fills an all-predicate entry and each predicate entry and returns the number of sources filled, not the number of entries; target-only nodes are not sources.
- A failed exclusive writer-lock probe, a no-lock-writer flag, or a generation change prevents that source from being counted as filled. A generation change detected after storing removes the source's new entries.
- The whole-graph stamp is replaced only when every visited source filled and the graph-version token stayed equal. Otherwise it is removed and readers use their per-source checks. Empty outgoing globals return zero and may have a current whole-graph stamp; a subsequent token change makes that stamp stale.
- At the pin a rebuild bumps the token after warming, making the whole-graph stamp stale at once even though the per-source entries remain valid; this departure remains [simp-str-003](../../Verus_verification/design_simplification.md#simp-str-003). Clearing entries alone while keeping a current stamp can return zeros ([F-0406](../../Verus_verification/bugs_issues.md#F-0406)).

structure.rebuilt.body: The interned snapshot, the two-hop statistics, the accelerator's snapshot and cached algorithm results are rebuilt stores. Each records the graph-version token it was built from and is current only while that token is still the live one, so a failed rebuild leaves it stale for every process.

structure.rebuilt.token.body: Every change to the adjacency index, to its edges or to its labels, increases the graph-version token; a write to node rows or properties alone does not. The token never decreases and a value is never reused, even when the write rolls back. A cached answer that also depends on other content must key on that content too or not be cached ([algorithm cache](algorithms.g5.md#algorithms.cache.token)).

structure.rebuilt.stamp.body:
A rebuilt store is current only when it carries a build stamp and that stamp equals the live token. A store that was never stamped is stale even while the token is still zero, and a store stamped at zero is current until the token moves.
- An unset token reads as zero, but an unset or empty stamp means "not known", never zero.
- Asking which of several stores are stale applies the same rule to each store, in the order asked.
- The two-hop count reader in ObjectScript and the Python freshness module apply this one rule.

structure.rebuilt.valid.body: A cached algorithm result is valid only while the token it was computed under is still the live token. The token is read before the computation starts, so a write during the computation leaves the result stale, never wrongly current.

structure.rebuilt.rollback.body: When a computation sees a write that is not yet committed and that write later rolls back, must the cached result be thrown away? The provisional answer is yes, because the degree cache and the rebuild already treat that case as unsafe. Today the cached result stays current until the next write (observed).

structure.rebuilt.stale_read.body:
A reader never answers from an interned snapshot known to be stale.

- After an erasure, the first algorithm that reads the snapshot rebuilds it once, under a lock, before it answers.
- A variable-length Cypher query that would read a stale snapshot raises an error asking for a rebuild.

structure.drift.body: A declared adjacency index cannot drift from its rows, and declaring it on an install that has drifted repairs the drift.

structure.rebuild.body: A rebuild recreates the adjacency index from the rows and then the interned snapshot from the index, and running it again is safe. With a declared index the adjacency never needs it; the interned snapshot still does after bulk loads and erasures.

structure.rebuild.failure.body: What may readers see when a rebuild fails partway? The provisional answer, from the degree-cache design, is that an early failure leaves the previous adjacency, and a later one leaves a partial index whose degree cache is cleared, never wrong.

structure.verify.body: `verify_graph` reports one graph's adjacency entries with no row behind them, its rows with no adjacency entry, and its current degree-cache entries that disagree with a recount. Its `ok` answers only whether this graph's adjacency agrees with its rows.

temporal.edge.body:
A temporal edge records when an event happened on a triple in one graph, with a weight and optional attributes.
- The timestamp is event time, not the time of writing; a write with no timestamp is stamped with the current time.
- At most one temporal edge exists at one set of coordinates.
- The unit is set by the entry point: the engine's interface counts seconds, and a millisecond entry point that the engine does not expose counts milliseconds; a bucket is five minutes in either.
- Both entry points use the same per-graph stores, so a caller must keep one unit per graph; IVG cannot detect a mix.
- The single Python API currently violates missing-time stamping: omission and None are sent as epoch zero; [clock resolution](#temporal.edge.clock) also distinguishes normal bulk zero from its fallback.

temporal.edge.clock.body:
Timestamp normalization and the selected writer determine the stored coordinate,
so fixed-coordinate repeatability requires the same resolved event times.

- Single Python omission, None and explicit zero reach the single writer as text zero and remain epoch zero; a normal bulk zero uses each item's current seconds.
- If the bulk endpoint is unavailable before writing, its single-edge fallback stores that same zero at epoch zero. Explicit positive timestamps retain event time on all three paths.
- Bulk items require a usable timestamp; all items are validated and normalized before the first write, while an empty batch succeeds with count zero.
- Numeric short alias `ts=0` defers to a supplied long `timestamp` alias, while text `ts="0"` keeps zero. A present None long alias can fail conversion where an absent long alias defaults to zero.
- On a duplicate explicit positive timestamp, normal bulk reports a collision and zero writes; fallback counts the successful single call and cannot report the collision. The stored existing event remains unchanged.

temporal.edge.graph-scope.body:
Every temporal store is kept per graph, and an operation on one graph never reads or changes another graph's temporal data.
- The default graph follows the same rules as a named graph.
- A graph name that cannot be stored safely, such as `"0"` or a name with control characters, is refused before anything is written.

temporal.owner.body: Only the time-index component may access the temporal stores; every other component uses its operations, so a change to the stored layout touches one place. A new cross-graph need becomes a new operation on that component.

temporal.write.body:
Writing a temporal edge stores it with its attributes, updates the statistics and the newest-event index, and asserts the [implied structural edge](#temporal.structural) unless the predicate is temporal-only in that graph. Each write runs in one of three modes, which differ only when the coordinates already hold an edge.
- Insert, the default for direct writes, keeps the existing edge and reports a collision.
- Update replaces the existing edge's weight and attributes.
- Skip keeps the existing edge and counts the write as skipped.
- A batch write reports how many edges were written, how many collided and how many were skipped.
- A single-edge write reports success even for a collision; a caller that must know writes a one-edge batch and reads its counts.
- A write can leave out the inbound entry for edges never read by target; inbound reads then cannot see that edge.
- Today a direct write opens no transaction of its own: alone it keeps what it wrote before a failure, and inside a caller's transaction it joins it, but a rollback leaves its statistics counted. Whether a failed write must leave nothing is [open](#temporal.write.partial-failure).

temporal.write.collision.body: An insert at coordinates that already hold an edge changes nothing anywhere, so the first write wins and the statistics never count the second write. This holds whether the earlier write came from an earlier call or from earlier in the same batch.

temporal.write.update-statistics.body:
What should the statistics say after an update replaces an edge's weight?
- Provisional answer, as documented: the statistics keep describing the first write.
- Alternative: they describe the edges as they are now, recomputed as after a delete.
- Alternative: every write counts, so an update adds a second count and its new weight.

temporal.write.repeatable.body:
Writing the same set of temporal edges into an empty graph, in any batch size, must leave every store identical, so a graph can be rebuilt from its source events.
- The order of writes does not matter either when colliding writes are identical and all timestamps of a triple carry one weight.
- The implied structural edge keeps the weight of the triple's first write.

temporal.write.partial-failure.body:
When a temporal write fails part way, what may it leave behind, and must a retry be able to finish it?
- Provisional answer, as documented: the parts written before the error stay, because a direct write runs no transaction.
- Alternative: a failed write leaves nothing, so a retry starts clean.
- Open either way: a retry in insert mode now finds the edge, reports a collision and never writes the missing structural edge, statistics or attributes.

temporal.write.retry.body:
A Counts error does not undo completed items: the Python store retries every
normalized item through the single writer and reports only accepted fallback calls.

- With a nonzero current clock, an error after a completed zero-timestamp item can leave both its current-time and epoch-zero events while reporting one write. A failure before any item writes leaves only epoch zero.
- A positive explicit timestamp collides at its original coordinate; fallback can report one accepted call while inserting nothing new and reporting no collisions.
- A completed prefix of a mixed zero/positive batch remains when the whole batch is replayed; the failed prefix's counters are discarded. This describes completed item boundaries and successful fallback calls, not a partial effect inside one write or a real transport failure.

temporal.write.concurrency.body:
Must first-write-wins, exact statistics and an exact newest-event index also hold when several writers touch the same coordinates or triple at once?
- Provisional answer: none. The recorded rules (first write wins, spec 254 Decision 2; the exact newest-event index, spec 255 Decision 1) name no exception for overlapping writers, but temporal writes take no lock. The lock rationale on record (ADR-0010) is about counters: locks held to commit deadlocked in an earlier design.
- A write racing a purge or delete of the same triple can leave a timestamp without its structural edge; this is recorded as a known open race.

temporal.stats.body:
The statistics summarize the temporal edges written to each bucket, so windowed counts, totals and extremes need not read every edge.
- An aggregate read answers exactly the requested window with both ends included.
- Buckets the window holds whole come from the statistics; a bucket the window cuts is read edge by edge.
- The distinct-target count is an estimate with an error of about a quarter.
- A velocity read counts one source's events, over every predicate, in the whole buckets that a recent window touches.
- A burst read lists every source whose velocity over such a window reaches a threshold.

temporal.stats.after-purge.body:
A raw purge keeps the statistics, so they go on describing the past after the edges they summarize are gone.
- Statistics are removed separately, by bucket range, and that never touches temporal edges.
- An aggregate read over a bucket cut by both the window and a purge counts none of the purged part.

temporal.stats.cut-bucket.body:
When a raw purge has cut a bucket and a surviving edge in that bucket is later deleted or its node erased, should the bucket's statistics keep the purged history or describe only the survivors? There is no provisional answer.
- Keep the history, as the purge rule says.
- Describe only the survivors, as the delete rule says; this is the current behavior, which leaves the event counter still holding the purged history.

temporal.latest.body:
IVG keeps the newest-event index up to date on every write, so a latest read never has to search all of time.
- A latest read returns each requested source's newest temporal edge with its attributes.
- The caller names sources, a source prefix, or neither for every source.
- An optional predicate narrows the edges; an optional cutoff excludes edges at or after it, and an optional look-back ignores edges older than the cutoff minus the look-back.
- Ties at the newest timestamp go to the last predicate and target in index order.
- A source with no qualifying edge is left out, never returned empty.
- A graph written before this index existed answers named sources by searching back through time, and refuses prefix and every-source reads until its index is rebuilt once.

temporal.latest.exact.body: The newest-event index must stay exact through every write, single-edge delete, purge, node erasure and graph erasure. Whether that includes overlapping writers is [open](#temporal.write.concurrency).

temporal.delete.body:
Deleting one temporal edge removes it and everything derived from it, and reports when there was nothing to delete.
- The statistics of its bucket are recomputed from the remaining edges, and its event counter goes down by one, except in a bucket a raw purge has cut ([open question](#temporal.stats.cut-bucket)).
- The newest-event index moves back to the newest remaining edge.
- When it was the triple's last timestamp, the structural edge follows [the end of the implication](#temporal.structural.end).

temporal.structural.body:
A temporal edge implies a structural edge for the same triple in the same graph. The triple is then visible to SQL, Cypher `MATCH`, edge counts and traversal while any of its timestamps exist.
- The structural edge comes with both endpoint nodes in that graph.
- [Temporal-only predicates](#temporal.optout) are the exception.
- This needs the adjacency index declared on the edge table. Without it, a write that names no graph leaves only an adjacency entry, which the next rebuild wipes; a write that names a graph also writes an unmarked structural edge and its nodes, which no temporal delete or purge removes and which ignore the temporal-only setting.
- Whether an explicit edge delete may remove a marked structural edge while timestamps remain is [open](#temporal.structural.explicit-delete).

temporal.structural.mark.body:
An implied structural edge carries the temporal mark, so counts, exports and later cleanup can tell it from an explicitly written edge.
- All timestamps of one triple share one structural edge.
- The mark, not a count of timestamps, decides whether the edge may be removed; the purge itself checks whether any surviving timestamp still holds the triple.

temporal.structural.adopt.body:
An explicit structural write of a triple that has a marked structural edge adopts it: the mark is cleared and the explicit write's qualifiers apply.
- Single and bulk edge creation, a Cypher `CREATE` or `MERGE` between matched nodes, and a ledger relationship create all adopt.
- After adoption, no temporal delete or purge removes the edge.
- An adopting `create_edge` reports True, unlike writing an existing unmarked edge again, which reports False.
- An explicit edge written before any temporal edge is never marked.
- Observed exception in Python `create_edge` and `store_edge`: caller qualifiers can supply `temporal=True`. A new row then keeps the mark; an adopting `create_edge` also keeps it when supplied again, and repeated marked creates report True and replace qualifiers. This conflicts with the unmarked explicit-edge rule above.

temporal.structural.end.body:
When a triple's last timestamp in a graph goes, by a delete or a purge, that graph's structural edge for the triple goes too while it still carries the mark.
- The rule is the same in the default graph and in every named graph.
- An unmarked structural edge stays.
- Endpoint nodes stay unless the purge is asked to [retire bare nodes](#temporal.purge.bare-nodes).

temporal.structural.upgrade.body:
When an install declares the adjacency index, every triple with temporal edges and no structural edge gets a marked one, except triples of temporal-only predicates.
- The upgrade never deletes rows and never registers predicates.
- It remembers a bounded number of triples and re-checks the ones it forgot, so it never misses a row.

temporal.structural.ledger.body:
A marked structural edge is derived from the time index, so it is outside ledger governance. Direct temporal writes create no revisions ([inside a changeset they do](#temporal.ledger)), and the ledger's starting snapshot and its verification both skip marked edges.
- Ledger strict mode does not change this: a temporal write still succeeds, and with the adjacency index declared it still writes the marked structural edge.
- Strict mode skips only the engine's older client-side structural step, which runs when the adjacency index is not declared.

temporal.structural.ledger-nodes.body:
Are the endpoint nodes that a temporal write creates, or that a purge retires, governed by the ledger?
- Provisional answer: none is recorded; only marked edges were declared outside governance.
- Alternative: treat such nodes like marked edges and skip them in the starting snapshot and verification.
- Alternative: govern them, so these node writes are refused or recorded while the ledger is on, and a purge never retires a node the ledger recorded.

temporal.structural.explicit-delete.body:
May an explicit edge delete remove a marked structural edge while its triple still has timestamps? There is no provisional answer.

- Today it does: the timestamps stay, and the next temporal write of the triple puts the edge back.
- The parent rule says the triple stays visible while any timestamp exists.

temporal.optout.body:
A graph can register a predicate as temporal-only, so that its temporal edges imply no structural edge in that graph.
- A predicate is structural until registered.
- A registration covers one graph and one exact predicate name; patterns are not supported.
- The choice is stored, not passed per write, so every writer, the upgrade and the purge give the same answer.
- A registration is configuration, not content: erasing a graph keeps it, erasing everything removes it, and snapshots carry it.

temporal.optout.effect.body:
A write of a temporal-only predicate stores only time-index data: no structural edge, no node and no adjacency entry.
- Traversal, degree, edge counts and Cypher `MATCH` over it find nothing.
- An empty structural read that names such a predicate logs one warning that names the reads that do work.
- Window, aggregate, newest-event and temporal Cypher reads keep working.
- An explicit structural create of the triple still writes a normal unmarked edge.

temporal.optout.toggle.body:
Changing a registration affects only later writes: existing structural edges stay until dropped, and missing ones stay missing until backfilled.
- Writers are never blocked; writes in flight while a predicate is registered may still add marked edges, which the drop removes.
- Backfilling writes the missing marked edges and their nodes for a predicate made structural again, using its temporal edges as the authority.
- Backfilling refuses a predicate that is still temporal-only, can be repeated safely, and needs the adjacency index declared.

temporal.optout.drop.body:
Dropping removes the marked structural edges of temporal-only predicates in one graph, and by default the nodes this leaves bare.
- A purge does not look for these edges, even ones written before the predicate was registered; removing them is the drop's job.
- The drop refuses a predicate that is still structural, because new writes would put the edges back.
- It removes only edges that still carry the mark when they are deleted.
- It runs in bounded transactions and can be resumed; a dry run counts and changes nothing.
- It needs the adjacency index declared.

temporal.optout.stranded.body:
What should happen to the marked structural edges of a predicate whose timestamps were purged while it was temporal-only, if it is made structural again before the drop? There is no provisional answer.
- Today no operation removes them: the drop refuses a structural predicate, and no timestamp is left for a delete or purge to find.
- Alternative: let a cleanup remove marked edges that no timestamp holds, whatever the registration says.
- Alternative: refuse to make a predicate structural again while its old marked edges remain.
- Related: should a single-edge delete leave such edges for the drop, as the purge does?

temporal.window.body:
A window read returns the temporal edges whose timestamps fall in a range, both ends included, ordered by timestamp, then source, predicate and target.
- It can return each edge's attributes in the same call.
- It reads a window of any size, page by page.
- A failed read raises an error and never returns a short or empty answer as if it were complete.
- It can filter by one source, a list of sources, a source prefix, a set of predicates and a direction.
- A list returns the union of its sources, each edge once; an empty list returns nothing.
- With a source filter, the cost depends on the sources asked for, not on every source active in the window.
- In the inbound direction the source filter names the target.
- The older one-call reads keep their arguments and output, and raise when a window is too large for one answer (about 35,000 edges).
- A reversed window, whose start is after its end, is empty, not an error.

temporal.window.sources.body:
Leaving the source filter out and passing an empty list of sources are different requests. Left out, the read covers every source in the window; an empty list covers none and returns nothing.
- The Python reader sends no `sources` key when the caller passes none, and sends an empty list when the caller passes one.
- The server reads every source only when the request names no source, no list and no prefix. A list that names nothing, or names only empty strings, reads nothing.
- Naming more than one of a source, a list and a prefix is refused before any server call.

temporal.window.paging.body:
Each page is read live from where the last page stopped, so the server holds only a resume point between pages. A reader is closed when the iteration ends or is abandoned; [releasing the reader](#temporal.window.paging.release) says exactly when its server handle is freed.
- An edge removed after a page was read is not returned later.
- Only a page marked done ends the read. An empty page that is not marked done does not end it: the reader asks for the next page.
- The events returned are the rows of every page, in order, up to and including the page marked done.
- A page holds at most the rows asked for (1,000 by default), and stops early once its text nears two million characters.

temporal.window.paging.release.body:
The server handle of a paged read is freed exactly once, by whichever comes first: the server's last page, the caller's close, a failed page, the end of a `with` block, or garbage collection.
- A window that fits the first page is answered and freed inside the opening call. That costs one round trip, and no close call follows.
- When a later page comes back marked done, the server has freed the handle itself, so the reader makes no close call either.
- Closing before the end sends one close call. Closing again, or after the last page, sends nothing, and the closed reader returns no more events.
- A failed page raises a temporal window error after one close call has freed the handle. A failed opening call raises at the call, and there is no reader to close.
- On the server, closing a handle that is not open does nothing, and asking for the next page of one raises an error instead of returning an empty page.
- A handle belongs to the process and connection that opened it: another connection cannot page it, and the handle is freed when that process ends.
- Today's server never sends an empty page that is not marked done: a page stops only at its row count, its size limit or the end of the window, and each of the first two holds at least one row.

temporal.window.concurrent-writes.body:
Must a paged read show one consistent moment when edges are written while it runs?
- Provisional answer: no, it is a live read, so an edge written ahead of the current page appears and one written behind it never does.
- Alternative: fix a snapshot bound when the read starts.

temporal.purge.body:
A raw purge removes one graph's temporal edges in a time range, with their attributes and the marked structural edges that only those timestamps held up.
- The range includes its start and excludes its end.
- Statistics and interned label sets stay.
- A triple with timestamps on both sides of the range keeps its structural edge.
- Structural edges go before temporal edges, so a purge that fails part way can be finished by running it again.
- The result reports how many edges were deleted and skipped, and how many nodes were retired when that was asked.
- The legacy whole-store purge acts on the default graph and also removes statistics of buckets before the cutoff's.

temporal.purge.bare-nodes.body:
A purge can also delete the endpoint nodes of the structural edges it removed, when they are left bare in that graph.
- Only those endpoints are candidates.
- A node that gains an edge, label or embedding while the purge runs is kept.
- The Python interface does this by default; the ObjectScript interface does it only when asked.
- A separate sweep removes bare nodes that an earlier purge left behind.

temporal.erase.body:
Erasing a graph removes all of its temporal data, erasing everything removes every graph's, and erasing a node removes its temporal edges at both ends in that graph.
- Node erasure keeps the remaining statistics and the newest-event index exact.
- Erasure of temporal data runs inside the erasure's transaction and changes no other graph.
- Today a prefix erase finds IDs through node rows, so a temporal-only event whose endpoints have no node row is not erased; erasing those IDs explicitly, or the whole graph, removes it.

temporal.ledger.body:
A changeset can include temporal edge writes, which the ledger applies in the same transaction as the changeset's other operations.
- A temporal write in a changeset defaults to update mode, unlike a direct write.
- The revision lists each temporal edge write.
- Direct temporal writes outside a changeset create no revision.

temporal.ledger.atomic.body: If a changeset fails, none of its temporal writes may remain, statistics included.

temporal.ledger.insert-collision.body:
What should an insert collision inside a changeset do?
- Provisional answer, as documented for changesets: fail the operation, and with it the commit.
- Today it changes nothing, the commit succeeds, and the revision still records a temporal edge write.
- Alternative: succeed without recording the write.

ledger.revision.body: Every revision is permanent and numbered. Seq numbers increase by one with no gaps, and each revision's parent is the revision before it.

ledger.lifecycle.body:
The ledger is off until someone enables it.

- The first enable writes a genesis revision that describes the current graph.
- Enabling a ledger that is already enabled changes nothing and returns the head.
- The first enable sets strict mode, the size limit for a changeset and the size bound for a reconstruction. Strict mode can be switched later.
- Disabling is safe to repeat. While the ledger is disabled, commits and redactions are refused with `LedgerDisabledError` and nothing is recorded. Before the first enable they are refused with `LedgerNotEnabledError`.
- Today, disabling does not cancel an unfinished redaction: its next batch is refused with `LedgerDisabledError`, the marker stays, and the caller runs the same redaction again after enabling. Whether disable should be refused instead is [open](#ledger.lifecycle.disable-during-redaction).
- Enabling again while a redaction is unfinished skips the adoption below without an error.
- Enabling again records the changes made while it was disabled as an adoption revision.

ledger.lifecycle.genesis.body: The genesis records every node, label and property in the namespace as default-graph content, and every relationship with its own graph. It leaves out the plain relationship row that a temporal edge creates, because the ledger does not govern that row. So a node ID held by two graphs gets two node-create records, and the labels and properties of both nodes are recorded under that one ID.

ledger.lifecycle.genesis.shared-ids.body:
How should the genesis treat a node ID that two graphs hold? Provisional answer: none recorded. Today the two nodes are merged under one ID, although a human decision says the same ID in two graphs is two nodes.

- Merging matches how verify compares nodes, but loses which graph held which label or property, against the decision that each graph's labels and properties are its own.
- When both graphs give the same property different values, which value the replay keeps and which one verify reads are not tied to each other, so verify could report a false difference.

ledger.lifecycle.disable-during-redactio.body: What should disabling the ledger do while a redaction is unfinished? There is no provisional answer. Today disable is accepted, the redaction's next batch is refused, and the caller must run the redaction again after enabling; that enable skips its adoption without an error.

ledger.changeset.body:
A changeset holds one or more operations in order: node, label, property, relationship, qualifier and temporal-edge changes.

- A reserved property name (`id`, `__graph`) is refused before anything is applied.
- A relationship is named by exactly one of these: its statement ID, its source, predicate, target and graph, or an earlier create in the same changeset.
- The same changeset always produces the same JSON form and the same fingerprint.

ledger.commit.body:
A commit applies a whole changeset as one new revision, or applies nothing. The exception is the changeset's [post-commit properties](#ledger.commit.post-commit), which are written after the revision and are not part of it.

- It returns the new revision, whether it was a replay, and the statement ID of each relationship it created, by operation position.
- A failing operation is reported by its zero-based position in the changeset.
- A relationship to a node that exists in no graph fails with `NodeNotFoundError`, unless the changeset asks for missing nodes to be created.
- Creating a relationship that already exists in its graph fails, unless the operation is an upsert, which merges the qualifiers. A temporal edge's plain row is taken over by the create instead.
- A revision, its records and its changes become visible together.
- The changes apply in order, each on top of the last. Two writes of one property in a changeset keep both records, prior value and new value each time, and the property shows the last value. Writing the value a property already has records nothing.
- The first change that fails stops the commit, and every earlier change of the changeset is rolled back with it: no revision, no record and no content change remains.

ledger.commit.admission.body:
A commit is checked in a fixed order before anything is applied. The order is: take the head lock, check that the ledger is enabled, check the idempotency key, check the expected head, check the size. So a retry that matches its idempotency key replays even when its expected head is now stale.

- A reserved property name is refused when the operation is added to the changeset. The server checks it again while applying, and a refusal there rolls the whole commit back.
- While a redaction is unfinished, the operations are applied first and then checked against its target. A commit with any record in the target is refused, and its transaction rolls back ([rule](redaction.g5.md#redaction.batches.commits)).

ledger.commit.serial.body: Commits run one at a time, so the history stays one chain even with many writers. A commit waits up to 30 seconds for the head lock and then fails with `LedgerLockTimeoutError`, which is safe to retry.

ledger.commit.expected-head.body: A changeset may name the head it expects. If another revision was committed first, the commit fails with `StaleHeadError`, names the current head and writes nothing. An expected head that is not a revision of this ledger fails with `UnknownRevisionError`.

ledger.commit.size.body: For a changeset commit, an empty changeset is refused with `EmptyChangesetError`. So is a changeset with more operations than the ledger's limit, with `ChangesetTooLargeError`; the limit is 50,000 unless set otherwise when the ledger is enabled.

ledger.commit.kind.body:
Should callers be able to choose a commit's kind? Provisional answer: no, it should be internal, because only verify needs the adoption kind.

- Today `commit` accepts any kind. A kind other than changeset skips the empty and size checks.
- The adoption kind records the given differences without changing the tables.
- Any other kind, such as `genesis` or `redaction`, is applied like a changeset but labeled with that kind.

ledger.commit.caller-transaction.body:
A commit made inside the caller's open transaction is part of that transaction. The caller's rollback removes the revision and its changes without leaving a gap in the numbering. The head stays locked until the caller's transaction ends.

- Enabling the ledger and redaction refuse to run inside a caller's transaction.

ledger.commit.post-commit.body:
A changeset can carry post-commit properties: default-graph node properties written after the revision, with `$REVISION_ID` replaced by the new revision's ID. They are not recorded in the revision, so verify reports them as unrecorded writes.

- Without a caller's transaction they are a second commit, so a failure keeps the revision and is returned in the result as `post_commit_error`, not raised.
- Inside a caller's transaction they join it, and the caller's rollback removes them with the revision.

ledger.commit.post-commit.recorded.body: Should post-commit properties be recorded in the ledger, left out of verify, or only documented as unrecorded writes? There is no provisional answer. Today they are unrecorded, verify reports them, and neither strict mode nor the block on commits into a target being redacted checks them.

ledger.idempotency.body:
A commit with the same idempotency key and the same fingerprint as an earlier revision returns that revision, marked as replayed, and changes nothing.

- The fingerprint covers only the actor, actor type and operations, so a retry with a new message or correlation ID still replays.
- The same key with different operations fails with `IdempotencyConflictError`.
- A key used only by a refused commit stays free.
- Two commits sent at once with the same key make one revision.
- A key whose revision was later redacted is refused instead ([rule](redaction.g5.md#redaction.idempotency)).

ledger.idempotency.key-required.body: Retry protection needs an idempotency key. A changeset without one is applied again when it is sent again.

ledger.node-scope.body:
The ledger keeps nodes in the default graph. Its node operations read and write only default-graph rows, and its node records name no graph. Relationship records name the relationship's own graph.

- One exception: a relationship created in a named graph adds bare node rows for its endpoints in that graph, if they are missing there. The database requires those rows. They get no node records.
- An endpoint counts as existing if its ID exists in any graph.

ledger.immutability.body: Revision rows cannot be changed or deleted, through SQL or through objects, and every record keeps its position. The only exception is redaction, which turns records into tombstones and empties four free-text fields ([exception](redaction.g5.md#redaction.metadata.exception)).

ledger.unrecorded.body: Graph writes made outside the ledger still work while it is enabled, but they create no records. Verify reports them, verify with adoption records them, and strict mode refuses them.

ledger.strict.body:
In strict mode, these engine calls are refused with `LedgerStrictModeError` and change nothing, so ledger commits are the engine's only way to change the governed graph, apart from a commit's own [post-commit properties](#ledger.commit.post-commit), which strict mode does not check. The [access rules](../concepts/access.g5.md#access.ledger_strict) say which callers and surfaces this governs.

- Node and edge writes: `create_node`, `store_node`, `create_edge`, `store_edge`, `set_edge_weight`, `delete_edge`, `delete_node`.
- Bulk writes: `bulk_create_nodes`, `bulk_create_edges`, `bulk_ingest_edges`, `bulk_delete_nodes`, `bulk_load_session`.
- Erases: `erase_graph` (and its old name `drop_graph`), `erase_all` and `delete_nodes_by_prefix`.
- Reifications and inference: `reify_edge`, `delete_reification`, `materialize_inference`, `retract_inference`.
- Imports and restore: `import_graph_ndjson`, `import_rdf`, `load_networkx`, `restore_snapshot`.
- Cypher through `execute_cypher` with any updating clause.
- The store's `write_nodes`, `write_edges`, `delete_nodes`, `delete_edges` and `erase_bare_nodes`.
- The bulk loader class and raw SQL are not guarded.
- A direct temporal-edge write is never refused, because strict mode does not govern direct temporal writes or their plain rows ([rule](temporal.g5.md#temporal.structural.ledger)). A temporal write inside a changeset is part of the revision ([temporal edges in a changeset](temporal.g5.md#temporal.ledger)).

ledger.strict.fail-open.body: When the engine cannot read the ledger's state, should a strict-mode check allow the write or refuse it? Provisional answer: none; today the check allows the write. A later fix treated one such case, a writer without access to the class dictionary, as a defect.

ledger.readers.body:
Readers show the ledger without changing it.

- History lists revisions in order and in pages. It can filter by actor, actor type, time, correlation ID and source.
- A revision's records come back in ordinal order, with prior and new values.
- A diff between two revisions gives the net change, nodes first, then relationships, each sorted by entity ID and attribute. The diff in the other direction is its exact inverse.
- Reconstruct returns the graph as of a revision. Above 250,000 nodes and relationships (set at enable) it refuses with `ReconstructionTooLargeError` unless asked to stream.
- Export writes a reconstruction as NDJSON that `import_graph_ndjson` accepts, with no size bound.

ledger.readers.history.body:
History filters the current revision rows before it sorts and limits a page. Oldest-first pages exclude the cursor sequence and everything older; newest-first pages exclude it and everything newer, while integer zero starts at the newest revision.
- A full nonempty page returns its last sequence as the next cursor, even when it is the final full page. A short or empty page returns no cursor, so an exactly full final page needs one extra empty read.
- Time bounds include equality. A filter set to None is omitted; empty text is still a supplied filter.
- Text comparisons follow the database: this provider accepts ASCII case changes and trailing spaces or tabs, but interior JSON spacing still matters for stored source text. Decoding that source for display is a separate step.
- A zero limit returns an empty page, and IRIS refuses a negative one. A failed read or required-field decode raises instead of becoming an empty page. Each acquired cursor gets one close attempt.
- Pages are live reads, not one fixed snapshot. Text "0" is tested as true before cursor conversion, so in newest-first order it selects sequences below zero instead of the initial page. The scope of exact text matching is [open](#ledger.readers.history.text-policy).

ledger.readers.history.text-policy.body: Should history text filters keep the database's case and trailing-space matching, or use binary string identity? Working answer: document current matching to preserve existing queries until the maintainer decides; binary matching would distinguish correlation IDs and source JSON text that currently compare equal. The API says "exact" for correlation IDs, but no source settles whether that requires binary matching.

ledger.readers.bound.body:
Ordinary reconstruction checks its size after each record, so it can refuse a history that grew above the limit even if later deletes make the requested graph small. Streaming reconstruction and export skip that check; both first build the whole requested graph in memory.

- The count is nodes plus relationships; labels and properties add no entities. Redaction tombstones and audit records change no content.
- A read stops at the named revision, so later records cannot change its content or cause its size refusal.
- Today a stored limit of zero is read as the default 250,000. Whether the limit should instead concern only the final graph is [open](#ledger.readers.bound.policy).

ledger.readers.bound.policy.body: Should reconstruction's limit cap every intermediate graph or just the requested graph? Working answer: keep the current check after each record and document it; the alternative is a final-size limit, which permits a history to use more memory before it shrinks.

ledger.readers.diff.body:
A diff selects records after the earlier revision through the later revision, including that later revision. Equal endpoints return no entries; reversing the endpoints swaps each entry's before and after values.

- Within one uninterrupted entity life, each changed attribute shows its first prior and last new value; if those match, the attribute contributes no entry.
- A life created and deleted inside the range contributes no entry. Deleting a life that existed before the range and then recreating it contributes separate deletion and creation entries.
- Node deletion carries its labels and properties in the deletion's JSON snapshot. The reverse existence entry keeps that snapshot; a separate property entry with an absent after value does not by itself say the old life lacked that property.
- As built, changing a property before deleting and recreating the node can lose the range's original value: the snapshot holds the value at deletion, and closing that life drops its earlier attribute prior. The promised net change remains the requirement; this [reported gap](../../Verus_verification/bugs_issues.md#bug-led-101) has no product repair here.

ledger.readers.diff.order.body:
May callers apply a diff in its listed order as a script? Working answer: treat it as a set of lifecycle-aware net entries, sorted for display; the alternative requires a defined application order, especially when deletion and creation have equal sort keys.

- The maintainer must ratify that choice and whether deletion snapshots describe the value at deletion or the range's starting value. Until then, report the actual snapshots and keep full endpoint reconstruction from lifecycle diffs unproved.

ledger.verify.body: Verify replays every revision from the first to the head and compares the result with the current tables. It reports `equal`, or `diverges` with the differences. When asked to adopt, it records the differences as an adoption revision so that the next verify is equal.

ledger.verify.meaning.body: "Verifiable" means that replaying the history gives the current store. No hash chain covers the records, and the commit fingerprint exists only to recognize retries.

ledger.verify.scope.body:
Verify compares the structural graph only.

- Nodes are matched by ID across all graphs, with their labels and properties. Reserved properties are left out.
- Relationships are matched by source, predicate, target and graph, with their qualifiers. Statement IDs are not compared.
- The plain relationship row of a temporal edge is left out on both sides, and the temporal index itself is not compared.

ledger.verify.consistency.body:
Must verify compare one consistent moment of the ledger and the tables? Provisional answer: verify is best-effort, so run it when writes are quiet.

- Today it reads both without a lock, and the adoption it commits names no expected head.
- So a commit made during a verify can show up as a difference or be recorded twice.

algorithms.owner.body: Every algorithm has an Owner, and IVG gives complete answers without Arno. No Owner is removed when a Native Reader is adopted.

algorithms.routing.body:
A call uses a Native Reader only when all of these hold; otherwise the Owner answers.

- The algorithm is one of PageRank, PPR, WCC, CDLP and subgraph.
- The proof record lists the algorithm.
- The loaded library reports a Reader Revision for it at or above the proof record's minimum.
- The call is within the scope the proof covers: today, the default graph only.
- The call runs in the namespace the library reads, today `USER` only; anywhere else the Owner answers, because the library would read another namespace's graph ([open question](#algorithms.routing.namespace)).
- PageRank also uses its Owner when the default graph is in multigraph mode or a node has no edge.

algorithms.routing.revision.body: Routing reads Reader Revisions only from the library's own capability report, and minimum revisions only from the proof record. It never uses the library's version string or a list written into IVG's code. A missing, failing or unreadable report means no Native Readers.

algorithms.routing.fallback.body: If a Native Reader fails, returns nothing or returns an unreadable answer, the Owner answers instead and the failure is logged. The caller never sees the native failure.

algorithms.routing.reload.body: When the library is replaced, routing reads the new library's report on its next load and never routes on the old library's revisions.

algorithms.routing.excluded.body: Betweenness always uses its exact directed Owner. The library's own breadth-first computation is not adopted until a separate decision.

algorithms.routing.named_graphs.body:
Can a default-graph call still use a Native Reader once a named graph holds edges? There is no provisional answer.

- The native readers may read an index that merges every graph, and the gate never tests that case.
- Plausible answers: route to the Owner whenever a named graph has edges, or record named-graph coverage in the proof.

algorithms.routing.namespace.body:
Should Native Readers work in any namespace? There is no provisional answer.

- Today they are used only in the `USER` namespace, because the library reads that namespace's data whatever namespace calls it.
- Every other namespace always gets the Owner, although the namespace is IVG's isolation unit.

algorithms.proof.body: The proof record ships with IVG and only the evidence gate writes it, never a person. An algorithm absent from it answers from its Owner, and a missing or invalid record sends every algorithm to its Owner, with a log entry.

algorithms.proof.gate.body:
The gate compares each Native Reader with its Owner, using that algorithm's equivalence rule, on at least four graph shapes and one tie-heavy graph, with five repeated calls each.

- The gate fails when the proof record claims a revision above what the installed library reports.
- Where the library is required, the gate must not skip because the library is absent.
- An algorithm that fails stays on its Owner and does not block the others.

algorithms.proof.build.body:
Does a proven Reader Revision hold for every build and platform of the library? There is no provisional answer.

- Routing ignores the build, but the proof record was made on one ARM build only.
- Plausible answers: the revision is the contract across builds, or routing also requires a proven build.

algorithms.proof.ungated.body: Must the evidence gate also cover the other algorithms Arno speeds up, such as triangle count, strongly connected components, k-core and Leiden? There is no provisional answer. Today they use Arno without a proof entry and fall back only on a library error.

algorithms.graph_scope.body: PageRank, WCC, CDLP and subgraph read the default graph only, while PPR and degree centrality can read a named graph. Procedures that read the index without a graph dimension refuse, naming the Python method to use, once a named graph holds an edge. Without that refusal they would answer from every graph merged.

algorithms.op.body:
Every algorithm answer includes every node of the graph, nodes with no edge too, and the n in any formula is the graph's node count. Ranked answers come highest first, and ties go by node ID in IRIS collation; two scores equal to 12 decimal places are a tie.

- A direction is `out` (along edges), `in` (against them) or `both` (the graph read as undirected).
- PageRank and PPR reject a damping factor outside (0, 1) or an iteration count below 1 with `ValueError` before reading data.
- Operations with a direction reject an unknown direction with `ValueError` before reading data.
- The exceptions to "every node" are betweenness, which lists only nodes that score above 0, and walks and subgraphs, which list what they reach.

algorithms.op.pagerank.body:
Global PageRank is textbook PageRank over every node of the default graph, returned as (node, score) pairs whose scores sum to 1.

- The damping factor is 0.85 and the run is 20 iterations by default. The count is fixed, not a convergence test, except that with Arno the walk also stops once converged.
- A node with no out-edges spreads its rank over every node.
- Known departure at the pin: the Owner silently returns at most 10,000 rows, so a larger result can omit nodes and sum to less than one. That violates the complete-answer requirement; cache admission does not repair it.
- Rank passes in proportion to edge count, so two edges from one node to another pass twice the rank of one.
- Given seeds, it returns personalized PageRank cut at this method's iteration count. Its `bidirectional` and `reverse_weight` options are accepted and ignored.

algorithms.op.ppr.body:
Personalized PageRank ranks every node of one graph by a walk that restarts at the seeds. It equals networkx's `pagerank` with that personalization, on the graph read as a multigraph.

- The walk restarts at the seeds evenly with probability 1 minus the damping factor (default 0.85), and otherwise follows an out-edge chosen evenly.
- Every edge counts: an edge under each relationship type, and each parallel edge of a multigraph.
- A node with no out-edges hands its score back to the seeds, so the scores sum to 1.
- It stops after `max_iterations` (100) or once the total change in one iteration is below N times `tolerance` (1e-6), N being the nodes holding a score.
- A repeated seed counts once, a seed that is not a node scores nothing, and a node the walk never reaches scores 0.0.
- `graph=` picks the graph and `exclude_predicates=` leaves relationship types out.

algorithms.op.ppr.completion.body: Completing a PPR answer with zero-score nodes must distinguish nodes the walk never reached from positive scores omitted by an earlier row limit. A caller's larger result limit must not turn a truncated positive score into zero.

algorithms.op.ppr.zero_ties.body:
When a positive PPR score rounds to zero at the ranking precision, should it share the zero nodes' ID tie or precede every true zero? There is no provisional owner answer.
- The general ranking rule uses12-decimal ties, while the PPR guide also says unscored zeros come after scored nodes.
- Native/store zero completion appends zeros; the Python fallback sorts the full node map. A tiny positive and an earlier zero ID can therefore select different second nodes under the same explicit limit2; either chosen policy must be consistent across these routes.

algorithms.op.wcc.body: Weakly connected components ignore edge direction and label each node with the smallest node ID of its component, in IRIS collation. Labels spread until none changes; an optional round limit raises an error if they are still changing when it is reached.

algorithms.op.cdlp.body:
